items.prompt: State what is meant by the stored program concept.
items.canonical_answer: A program's instructions are held in the computer's memory, in the same memory as its data, so the processor carries out a program by fetching its instructions from memory one at a time, and the computer changes its task by loading a different program.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - the program’s instructions are held in memory like its data, so the machine is changed by loading a program, not rewiring.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why the stored program concept lets one machine do many jobs.
items.canonical_answer: Because the instructions are held in memory like data, what the machine does is decided by the contents of its memory, so loading a different program turns the same hardware into a different machine. One computer can run payroll in the morning, a game at lunch and a calculation in the afternoon, with nothing rewired, because the program is data that can be changed.
marking_guidance: Reason: what the machine does is decided by the contents of its memory - 1 mark.
Purpose: so a new program makes the same hardware a new machine, because loading it is all the change that is needed - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A school office runs a payroll program and then a report program on the same computer within the hour. Explain how this is possible without any change to the hardware.
items.canonical_answer: Both programs are stored in the one memory as instructions, following the Von Neumann model, and the processor fetches and executes whichever program is loaded. Moving from payroll to reports means loading the other program into memory, not changing the machine, so the same hardware does both jobs because what it does is decided by the contents of its memory.
marking_guidance: Context: this office’s two programs on the one machine - 1 mark.
Reason: because the stored program concept makes the task a matter of memory contents, loading the report program is all the change that is needed, so the hardware needs none - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: State what the Program Counter holds.
items.canonical_answer: The Program Counter (PC) holds the memory address of the instruction that will be fetched next.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - the address of the next instruction to be fetched, not a count of instructions.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Describe the difference between a general purpose register and a special purpose register.
items.canonical_answer: A general purpose register is one the program may use for its own working values, chosen as the program needs, whereas a special purpose register has one fixed role the program does not choose: the PC always holds the next instruction’s address and the MAR always holds the address being accessed. Both are fast stores inside the CPU, whereas what they may hold differs: anything useful, or one named thing.
marking_guidance: Difference: the program’s choice versus one fixed role - 1 mark per side, whereas both are registers inside the CPU, and both sides are needed.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: During a fetch, the processor copies the PC to the MAR, adds 1 to the PC, reads the instruction at the addressed location into the MDR, and copies the MDR to the CIR. Write the four register transfers, using register transfer notation.
items.canonical_answer:
[MAR] ← [PC]
[PC] ← [PC] + 1
[MDR] ← [[MAR]]
[CIR] ← [MDR]
marking_guidance: Context: this fetch on the given system - 1 mark per correct register transfer, up to 3 from the four written, with the double brackets on the memory read.
Reason: each transfer follows the described step, because the notation’s arrows name what moves where, so the four statements carry the marks.

items.prompt: A learner writes that the program counter counts how many instructions have been executed. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The PC does not count instructions; it stores the memory address of the instruction that will be fetched next. The test: is the value an address? It must be, because the PC’s value is copied into the MAR at the start of every fetch, and the MAR holds an address.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the PC has been given a counting job, when it holds the address of the next instruction to fetch.
1 mark: the correction with the test - its value is copied to the MAR at every fetch, so it must be an address.

items.prompt: State the purpose of the Arithmetic and Logic Unit.
items.canonical_answer: The ALU performs the program’s arithmetic and logic operations - such as addition, subtraction and comparisons - placing its result in the accumulator and setting the status flags.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - the unit that computes arithmetic and logic results into the accumulator.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why the Control Unit is needed to execute an instruction.
items.canonical_answer: An instruction in the CIR says what must happen but does nothing by itself: the control unit decodes it and sends the control signals that make the right components act, telling memory to read, registers to pass their contents, or the ALU to operate. Without the control unit, a decoded instruction would have no way of becoming the sequence of actions the CPU takes, which is why the decoding and signalling are its job.
marking_guidance: Reason: the instruction must be decoded and turned into control signals - 1 mark.
Purpose: so the other components act in the right order, because the signals are what carry the instruction’s meaning to them - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A program instruction requires two values to be added and the result stored. Explain the parts the ALU and the Control Unit play in executing it.
items.canonical_answer: The control unit decodes the instruction in the CIR and sends control signals that bring the two values to the ALU and prepare the store’s destination. The ALU performs the addition, places the result in the accumulator and sets the status flags, so the unit that decides and signals is the control unit and the unit that computes is the ALU, which is each one’s role in this instruction.
marking_guidance: Context: this addition instruction in the given program - 1 mark.
Reason: because the control unit signals the preparation and the ALU computes the total, the two parts share the work, so the instruction executes through each one’s role - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Asked to describe the role of the control unit, a learner describes the whole CPU. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The control unit is one part of the CPU, not the whole: the CPU includes the ALU, the registers and the control unit. The control unit decodes the instruction in the CIR and sends control signals to the other components; the arithmetic is done by the ALU and the holding by the registers, which are not the control unit’s job. The test: remove the ALU and the registers - what is left to do? The decoding and the signalling that remain are the CU’s job.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the whole CPU has been described for one of its parts, the control unit.
1 mark: the correction with the test - the CU decodes and signals, while the ALU computes and the registers hold, so removing the others leaves the CU’s job.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Describe how the three buses are used when the processor reads a value from memory.
items.canonical_answer: The address of the wanted location is placed on the address bus, a read signal travels on the control bus, and the value at that address travels back on the data bus into the MDR. Address out, signal out, data back: each bus carries one kind of thing, because the address is an address, the read command a signal, and the value data.
marking_guidance: Order: the steps in sequence - address first, then the read signal, then the value back - each statement a mark point, up to 2 from a longer list.
Input: the read starts from the given address in the MAR.
Result: the value ends up in the MDR, having travelled on the data bus.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain how a wider data bus moves data faster.
items.canonical_answer: The data bus carries as many bits as it has lines, so a 32-bit bus moves 4 bytes per transfer and a 64-bit bus 8 bytes per transfer for the same number of transfers. Doubling the width doubles the bits moved per transfer, so larger values or more data cross in one pass, which is why the width is a performance factor.
marking_guidance: How the width works: more lines carry more bits per transfer - 1 mark.
Because 4 bytes travel where 8 now do, the same transfer moves twice the data, so the width feeds the system’s speed - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes that the instruction being fetched travels on the control bus. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The control bus carries control and timing signals, such as read and write; the instruction is data, and data travels on the data bus. The test: name what travels - an address, a value, or a signal such as read or write. An instruction is a value, so its bus is the data bus, which is where the fetched instruction travels into the MDR.

1 mark: the correction with the test - name what travels: the instruction is a value, so it travels on the data bus.

items.prompt: State what the Status Register holds.
items.canonical_answer: The Status Register holds flags about the most recent operation, such as whether the result was zero, negative or caused overflow.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - flags describing the last result, such as zero, negative or overflow.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: State one factor, other than the clock speed, that contributes to a computer system’s performance.
items.canonical_answer: Cache memory: it holds a copy of the instructions and data the processor is most likely to need next, and a cache hit is reached far faster than a main-memory fetch, so the processor waits less.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - a factor named with its effect, cache or bus width or cores, because the effect is what makes it a performance factor.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain the effect on a computer's performance of increasing the cache size.
items.canonical_answer: When the cache is larger, a larger share of the instructions and data the processor needs next is already held in it, so fewer fetches go to main memory. A cache hit is reached far faster than a main-memory fetch, so the processor waits less often, which means more instruction stages complete per second - that is the chain from cache size to performance.
marking_guidance: Change: a larger cache holds more of what is needed next - 1 mark - so the effect is fewer slow main-memory fetches, because a hit is served from the fast store.
Consequence: the processor stalls less, which means more instructions complete per second, so the result is higher performance for the same clock - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A shop's till runs one program at a time, and the owner is offered a till with four cores. Explain why the till's single program will not run four times faster.
items.canonical_answer: The four cores can run instructions from separate programs at the same time, but the till runs one program whose instructions depend on each other’s results and must be executed in order. Extra cores speed up a computer that runs several programs at once; a single program does not speed up unless it is written to split its work across them, so the till’s work stays at one core’s pace, which is why the offer is wasted on this use.
marking_guidance: Context: this till and its single program - 1 mark.
Reason: because cores run separate programs together and the one program’s instructions are sequential, the extra cores idle, so the speed is unchanged - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Describe how USB provides connection to peripheral devices.
items.canonical_answer: USB is a standard port and cable system through which a wide range of peripherals attach - a keyboard, a storage device, a printer, a camera - and the devices are recognised when plugged in. One port type serves many devices, and devices can be attached and detached while the computer runs, which is what makes USB the everyday connection for peripherals.
marking_guidance: Order: the stages in sequence - plug in, the system recognises, the device is used - each statement a mark point, up to 2 from a longer list.
Input: the connection starts from the given peripheral and the USB port.
Result: the device ends up attached and usable, which is what the standardisation buys.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain how the choice between HDMI and VGA is made when connecting a display.
items.canonical_answer: HDMI carries digital video and audio on one cable, so a digital display receives the picture as sent and its sound with it. VGA carries analogue video signals only, so the computer’s digital picture must be converted to analogue before the cable and back to digital inside the display, and any sound needs a separate connection. A digital display with an HDMI port takes HDMI, because the two conversions are avoided and the sound rides along.
marking_guidance: How the two work: HDMI is digital with audio, VGA is analogue video only - 1 mark.
Because the VGA route needs two conversions and a second cable for sound, the digital display takes HDMI, which is what the choice turns on - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Describe the fetch stage of the Fetch-Execute cycle, using register transfer notation.
items.canonical_answer:
[MAR] ← [PC] - the address of the next instruction is copied to the MAR.
[PC] ← [PC] + 1 - the counter moves on to the following instruction.
[MDR] ← [[MAR]] - the instruction at the addressed location is read into the MDR.
[CIR] ← [MDR] - the instruction is copied to the CIR, ready to be decoded.
marking_guidance: Order: the transfers in sequence, first the MAR, then the increment, then the read, then the CIR - each statement a mark point, up to 2 from the four.
Input: the fetch starts from the given PC value, which is an address.
Result: the instruction ends up in the CIR, ready for the decode stage.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain how the decode and execute stages carry out the instruction in the CIR.
items.canonical_answer: Decode: the control unit interprets the instruction now in the CIR and sends control signals to prepare what it needs - operands fetched, registers opened, memory ready. Execute: the instruction is carried out - the ALU performs an arithmetic or logic operation and places the result in the accumulator, or a value moves between registers or memory. Each stage turns the instruction one step closer to its effect, which is how the cycle executes what was fetched.
marking_guidance: How decode works: the CIR’s instruction is interpreted and signals are sent - 1 mark.
Because the execute stage then acts on the prepared parts, the instruction’s effect happens, so the two stages carry the fetched instruction through - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

| Execute | (c) | (d) |

marking_guidance: Context: this ADD instruction in the given cycle - 1 mark per completed entry, (a), (b), (c), (d).
Reason: each entry names the stage’s work and registers, because the fetch moves the instruction, the decode prepares it and the execute computes it, so the four entries carry 4 marks.

items.prompt: A learner writes the fetch’s memory read as [MDR] ← [MAR], saying the MDR receives the MAR’s contents. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: [MDR] ← [MAR] would copy the address itself into the MDR. The fetch needs the value stored at that address, so the transfer is [MDR] ← [[MAR]]: square brackets mean ‘contents of’, and two pairs mean ‘contents of the address held in’. The test: what should arrive in the MDR - an address or an instruction? An instruction, so the double brackets are what write it.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the single brackets copy the address, when the value at that address was meant, a confusion of one bracket level with two.
1 mark: the correction with the test - [MDR] ← [[MAR]] fetches the contents of the addressed location, because two pairs mean contents of the address held in.

items.prompt: State what is meant by an interrupt.
items.canonical_answer: An interrupt is a signal that makes the processor pause its current program, run an interrupt service routine for that interrupt’s cause, and then resume the interrupted program.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - a signal that pauses the program for its own routine, then resumes the program.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why interrupts are used rather than the processor waiting for input.
items.canonical_answer: Waiting wastes the processor: while a key is awaited or a printer finishes, nothing else would run. An interrupt lets the processor work on another program and be signalled the moment input arrives or a device needs attention, so it responds to events as they happen instead of asking over and over, which is what interrupts buy: responsiveness without waiting.
marking_guidance: Reason: waiting would idle the processor while input is pending - 1 mark.
Purpose: so the processor works on other programs and is signalled when input arrives, because the interrupt carries the news without the asking - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A word processor's spelling checker can be cancelled mid-check by a key press. Explain how an interrupt makes this possible.
items.canonical_answer: The key press sends an interrupt signal; at the next check during the fetch-execute cycle the processor pauses the spelling check, runs the interrupt service routine for the keyboard, which reads the pressed key, and then resumes the interrupted program, which now sees the cancel request and stops the check. The key is noticed without the checker asking for it, which is what the interrupt arrangement does here.
marking_guidance: Context: this spelling checker and its given cancel key - 1 mark.
Reason: because the key press raises an interrupt serviced between instructions, the checker learns of the cancel without waiting to ask, so the cancel works mid-check - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes that one interrupt service routine handles every interrupt. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: Each cause of interrupt has its own service routine: a key press needs the key read, a printer out of paper needs the paper path handled, a timer needs the count reset. One routine cannot do all these, and the processor checks the interrupt’s priority before servicing it, because some events must be answered at once and others can wait. The test: would a printer out of paper and a key press need the same code? No, so each cause carries its own routine.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - one routine has been given every interrupt, when each cause needs its own code.
1 mark: the correction with the test - each cause has its own ISR and the priority is checked before servicing, because a key press and a printer fault need different handling.
items.provenance: Authored for 9618 AS from the topic 4.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
A clinic’s reception computer records patients while a nurse types. While she types, the printer signals that it has finished a page, and a timer reminds the system to save the open record every two minutes.
(a) Identify the special purpose registers used during the fetch of each instruction, and state what each holds. [2]
(b) Explain the role of the control unit in executing the instruction that saves the open record. [2]
(c) Explain how the printer’s signal and the timer’s reminder are handled while the typing continues. [4]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) The PC holds the address of the next instruction; the MAR holds the address being accessed; the MDR holds the data or instruction travelling to or from memory; the CIR holds the instruction being executed.
(b) The control unit decodes the save instruction in the CIR and sends control signals: the record’s destination address is placed in the MAR, a write signal goes to memory on the control bus, and the record’s data passes from the MDR onto the data bus, so the decoding and the signalling are what carry the save out.
(c) Both events are interrupts. The printer’s finish and the timer’s expiry each raise an interrupt; during the fetch of each instruction the processor checks for them, and services an enabled interrupt by pausing the typing program, running the event’s own service routine - the printer routine reports the finished page, the timer routine saves the record - and resuming the typing where it left off. The priority is checked before servicing, because a save reminder can wait a moment while the record is safe, so the typing continues almost unbroken while the events are handled.
marking_guidance: Part (a): identify the registers with what each holds - 2 points, one per register correctly identified with its contents.
Part (b): the reason the save executes - the control unit decodes and signals the write - 2 points: the decoding, the signals named.

Part (c): the context of this reception computer - each event is an interrupt with its own routine, checked for at the fetch and serviced with priority - 4 points: both interrupts named, the check during fetch, the separate routines, the resumption.

context.situation: A clinic reception computer handles typing, printing and saving at once.
